en: [1. Bhūmiparigrahaḥ] He is requested by four disciples in the form of Mohavajra-Yama and others, whose hands are occupied with the playful bearing of the vajra and vajra-bell, and whose sprout-like hands likewise hold the vajra and vajra-bell.
You are the nature of the vajra of delusion, Yamāri, the most terrifying;
you are the Teacher composed of all Buddhas, O Vajra Body—homage be to you!
You are the nature of the Vajra of Divisiveness, Yamāri, the most terrifying;
resembling the Vajra of Mind, O Ratnavajra, homage be to you!
You are the self-nature of passion-vajra, the lord who is the source of the phenomena of passion;
O supreme among all excellent sounds, homage be to you, Vajra of Speech!
You are Yamāri, whose nature is the Vajra of Envy, the performer of all rites;
you resemble the Vajra of Body, O sword-wielder, homage be to you!
You are the self-nature of all Buddhas, the singular synthesis of all Buddhas;
O Lord of the Maṇḍala, supreme among the most excellent of all Buddhas, homage be to you!
"O Lord, let the mandala that destroys all sins be drawn—
the formidable Yamaghna-maṇḍala, the sovereign of all maṇḍalas."

Having understood their supplication with a single sound and having seen the entire realm of sentient beings agitated by the afflictions such as passion and the rest, the yogi becomes enraged toward those afflictions.

With the mantra *hūṃ vajrottiṣṭha*, he raises his own wheel; illuminating all directions and surveying the three worlds, he causes the moon from the left eye (*makāra*) and the sun from the right eye (*ṭakāra*) to shine, and he should circumambulate the ground of the wheel.

Visualizing a blazing vajra on the soles of his feet, intent on brandishing the vajra and ringing the bell, dancing with playful grace upon vajra-footsteps, and roaring with the *hrīḥ* and other syllables from his throat, he terrifies the circles of obstructors and all wicked deities and the like.
"Listen, O multitudes of all obstacles residing in body, speech, and mind!
I am the glorious Yamāntaka, the one who employs the protection wheel."
With a vajra of blazing form, I shatter those born of the three bodies;
if anyone should transgress against me, they shall be shattered here, and not otherwise.
In place of the vajra, one should insert the wheel-jewel, the lotus, the sword, and so forth, and recite [the mantra].
Immediately after the consecration of the ground, one should drive in stakes to ensure there are no obstacles. In this regard, the mantra for driving in the stakes is as follows:
Oṃ gha gha ghātaya sarvaduṣṭān phaṭ | kīlaya kīlaya sarvapāpān phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ | Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: drive in the vajra-body, speech, and mind of all obstructors, hūṃ phaṭ!
With Yamāri, who holds a downward-pointing spear and an upward-pointing sword and vajra, one should nail down all obstacles in all directions;
this is the appropriation of the site.

[2. Consecration of the Earth] Having seen that the earth is free from obstacles, one should perform the binding of the boundary and so forth with the radiance of sharp flames. Then, having invoked her—one who is yellow in color, adorned with various ornaments, with her body half-risen, her right hand in the gesture of accepting a vow, and holding a vase in her left—one should worship her with various flowers, fragrances, and the like, and consecrate her [with the mantra]:
"O Goddess, you are the witness for all those who follow the Buddhas."
Just as the power of Māra was shattered by the Protector Śākyasiṃha through the specific practices of the vehicle and the stages and perfections,
so too, having conquered the power of Māra, I shall draw the mandala.
Then, one should contemplate her as dissolved right there.
Thus is the consecration of the earth.

[3. The Descent of Dust] Then once again, having scattered a profusion of various flowers upon that ground smeared with fragrance, and having fashioned mandalas with moon-disks and so forth at the locations of the deities, one should invoke the wheel there by means of the light-rays of the heart-wisdom (*hṛjjñāna*), perform the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandhana*) and other rites, and carry out the worship, praise, and tasting of the nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*). Then, placing the right knee-cap upon the earth and raising an incense burner with the right hand, one should supplicate the Perfectly Awakened Ones within the wheel:
"O Blessed One, Yamāri, true Vajra, King of Knowledge (*vidyārāja*), homage be to you!"
O Lord, compassionate by nature, I desire to write down the maṇḍala.
Out of compassion for your disciples and for your own worship,
O Blessed One, you ought to grant your grace to me, your devotee.
May the Buddhas, who bestow the purposeful activity of the wheel of the world, take heed of me;
as well as the Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, and whatever other mantra-deities there may be.
The deities, the world-protectors, and the spirits who have been instructed in perfect enlightenment—
whatever beings there may be who delight in the teaching and possess the vajra-eye.
I, [name], the Great Vajrin, shall draw the maṇḍala of Kṛṣṇayamāri according to my capacity and with proper ritual offerings, for the purification of the world.
Out of compassion for me and my disciples,
you all should together grant your presence within the mandala.
Having thus performed this three times and having worshipped that wheel, one should place it in the sky.

Then, the yogin—having generated the moon and sun from the syllable *jaḥ*—together with a thread-laying master (sūtradhāra) who is a Khaḍgayamārin, should lay out five threads smeared with fragrant substances. These threads are colored according to the [deities], produced from the seed-syllables of Mohavajrayamāri and the others, differentiated into twenty-five types, twice as long as the mandala, and divided into twenty parts for the doors. Having caused the Tathāgatas, drawn in by the hook of a blazing gaze, to enter, [he should proceed].
With this mantra: *oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśe jaḥ*.
Then: *oṃ āḥ prayaccha sūtra mohakālāre svacakrasūtraṇāya hūṃ*.
And so on, up to the point of entreating the Enemy of the Time of Hatred (*dveṣakālāri*).

Reciting "Oṃ Āḥ! All phenomena are mutually interpenetrated; all phenomena are utterly merged! Hūṃ!", he sends forth the thread with three *jaḥ* syllables. Having himself recited "Ja Ja Jaḥ," he takes the thread above the navel with his left fist. Standing in the west facing east, together with [the assistant] standing in the east facing west, he should drop the sky-thread (*khasūtra*).
Again, the lower thread:
Oṃ āḥ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ | The time has come for you to come here for the sake of sentient beings.
Thus, exhorting the Tathāgatas dwelling in the sky with the sound of the thread, one should strike the eastern-western brahma-thread.
Facing north, one should strike the north-south brahma-thread with [the cord] facing south.

The Yakṣa-faced [deity] stationed in the southeast, together with the Preta-faced [deity] stationed in the northeast, [draws] the eastern root-line; the Preta-faced [deity] stationed in the northwest, together with the Yakṣa-faced [deity] stationed in the southwest, [draws] the western root-line; the Nāga-faced [deity] stationed in the southeast, together with the Indra-faced [deity] stationed in the southwest, [draws] the southern root-line; the Indra-faced [deity] stationed in the northwest, together with the Nāga-faced [deity] stationed in the northeast, [draws] the northern root-line. By this very method, on both sides of the two Brahma-lines, seven lines each are drawn, and outside of the root-lines, six lines each.

Thereafter, having doubled the two corner-lines corresponding to the archways (*toraṇa*), one should, starting from the northeast direction and proceeding clockwise while visualizing the equality of all directions, lay down two lines for the wheel-shaped vajra-garland. If there is no vision of the signs (*animitta*), there is no accomplishment. If the line is broken, it is the ruin of the preceptor. From the fault of deficiency or excess, disease arises. If there is confusion regarding the directions, the disciples will fall into error.

The outer maṇḍala is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways (toraṇas), joined by four lines, and decorated with necklaces, half-necklaces, ribbons, and so forth; it is inlaid with vajras and jewels at all corners, gates, projections, and joints.

Within the maṇḍala, occupying half its area, is a square central hub (varaṭaka) marked with a double-vajra (viśvavajra) and surrounded by a garland of vajras; from there, one should divide it into five [sections] each up to the gates according to the appropriate proportions, using the gaze of the Wrathful One (Krodha) associated with the syllable *dhīḥ*.
The gate of the mandala should be known by the great-souled ones as being one-eighth of its size,
excluding the magnificent and well-proportioned great altar (mahāvedī).

The *niryūhas* (projecting porticos) are to be known as being like doors; likewise is the *daivatapaṭṭikā* (deity-band), which is joined with *vajra*-apsarases and with dances accompanied by song, instrumental music, and so forth.
The altar (vedī) is half the width of the door; likewise are the cheeks (kapola) and wings (pakṣa).
There are also the necklaces (hāra), half-necklaces (ardhahāra), garlands of the sun (mārtaṇḍasraj), garlands of the moon (somamālā), and the fillet-band (paṭṭikā).
The ground for the dust-particles is half of that [the central area], outside the ground for the root-line;
the ground for the jeweled pillars and the other decorative bands is equal to the ground for the dust-particles.
The archway (toraṇa) should be three times the width of the door and provided with banners and bells;
with bells and banners fluttering in the wind, they should be placed at the outer corners.
For others, the arrangement is according to the wheel and as is aesthetically pleasing,
beginning with one cubit and extending up to a thousand cubits.
Having thus outlined [the mandala] in this sequence, one should, by means of the previous procedure itself, energize the powders with a blazing gaze and consecrate them with the mantra:

*oṃ vajracitra samaya hūṃ*. Then, the yogin, who is Yamāntaka of the nature of intrinsic reality (*svabhāva*), free from all conceptual constructions, standing within the wheel and taking his position in the northeast direction, should cast [the powders] with his left fist.

One should draw lines from the interior that are white, yellow, red, green, and black, making the width of the door twenty equal parts, and ensuring they are free from all defects such as being thick and so forth. In this regard, if the lines are thick, there will be disease; if thin, loss of wealth; if crooked, enmity; and if broken, death. The lines should be drawn with an interval of one barley-corn (*yava*) between them.
One should draw the eastern part as great white, the southern joined with yellow,
the western portion red, and the northern joined with madder-red;
the central ground should be depicted with the luster and form of a sapphire.

Having thus drawn the mandala, one should place universal lotuses (*viśvapadma*) in the positions of all the deities. In the center, there is a fierce blue five-pronged vajra upon a sun disk; at the base of the eastern spoke, a white eight-spoked wheel; at the base of the southern spoke, a green nine-faceted jewel upon a sun disk; at the base of the western spoke, a red eight-petaled lotus upon a sun disk; at the base of the northern spoke, a dark green sword upon a sun disk; a wheel in the southeast corner [of the outer square] marked by a double-vajra; a vajra in the southwest corner; a lotus in the northwest corner; a sword in the northeast; and [a wheel] at the eastern gate.

One should draw a twenty-spoked vajra-mallet at the southern gate, a white staff at the western gate, a lotus at the northern gate, and a sword; furthermore, one should draw four skull-cups in the four corners of the mandala.
Thus ends the falling of dust.
[4. Maṇḍalasādhana] Having thus beheld the completed maṇḍala, the yogin, through the union of his own limbs, causes the Buddhas to enter into himself;

pervading the expanse of space with that mind, he brings forth the maṇḍala, releases it, and establishes it in its proper place. Then, having performed the empowerment of the eyes and so forth, as well as the empowerment of the body and so forth, and having brought in the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra), offered the water for honor (argha) and other offerings, drawn it in by means of the wrathful deities, caused it to enter, bound it, and subdued it, he should cause the worship, praise, and tasting of nectar to be performed, and then, having recited the mantra and meditated upon it, he should satisfy it.
Having offered the bali-oblation and worship to the guardians of the directions, one should personally circumambulate the mandala and perform prostration.
Thus concludes the mandala practice.

[5. Consecration of the Vases] Then, having visualized eighteen vases—marked with the symbols of the presiding deities and the four maṇḍala deities, their necks covered with cloth, containing sprouts of mango and other trees, endowed with the five jewels, the five medicinal herbs, and the five grains, and appearing in the form of the maṇḍala circle produced by their respective mantras—one should perform the empowerment of their eyes and so forth, as well as their consecration; then, having invited the wisdom-circle (*jñānacakra*), offered the water for welcoming (*argha*) and other offerings, drawn it in, caused it to enter, bound it, and brought it under control, one should contemplate the worship and other rites.

Having placed a vajra bound with garlands upon their heads, one should recite the respective mantras three times at each junction of the day as long as desired, and then perceive that wheel right there in the form of water.
Thus concludes the consecration of the jar.
[6. Homa] Thereafter, one should perform the fire offering (homa) for the purpose of pacifying defects such as deficiencies and for the sake of increasing the merit of the patron.

In that regard, like the *śāntika* hearth, the all-purpose (*sārvakarmika*) hearth measures one cubit and is dug half a cubit deep. Leaving aside four finger-breadths from the edge of the excavation, it is surrounded by an altar (*vedi*) shaped like a fully blossomed lotus, measuring four finger-breadths in width and depth. Beyond that, it is surrounded by a square altar two finger-breadths wide. At its corners, upon half-moons, are three-pronged vajras. In the center of the hearth is a five-pronged vajra of hatred, measuring eight finger-breadths and one finger-breadth in height.

In the east, south, west, and north, one should fashion a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, and a sword, each six finger-breadths in size. Then, outside of that, one should fashion a circle of vajras, encircled by white powder; such is the fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

Then, the yogin, standing facing the east, having placed all the substances to be offered on the right side and having placed the aforementioned vessel for the arghya water and so forth on the left, should bring fire from the house of a brahmin or from the kitchen of a monastic community.
One should kindle it with fuel from milk-tree wood by fanning it; having consecrated it with the three-syllable mantra, one should thereafter offer the *kuśa* grass in a clockwise direction.

Then, preceded by the transformation into Vajradhara, one should meditate upon fire arising from the syllable *raṃ* on a triangular fire-pit atop a universal lotus (*viśvapadma*). This fire is white in color, possesses three faces, and has the bodies of two of one's own vidyās. It holds a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in its right hand and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the other; in the left hands, it holds a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and in the remaining two, a flaying knife (*kartṛ*) and a skull-cup (*karoṭa*). Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, it is adorned with the ornaments of a wrathful deity. Having visualized this, one should summon the wisdom-fire (*jñānavahni*) from one's own seed-syllable located in the heart, and having offered the water for the guest (*argha*) and so forth with the mantra "Oṃ ṭakki hūṃ jaḥ" using the hook-gesture (*aṅkuśamudrā*), one should proceed.

Having caused [the deity] to enter at the proper time and performed the worship and other rites, one should place the syllable *repha* (ra) in its mouth and offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Visualizing the syllable *yakāra* (ya) in the mouths of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should offer all the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) in due order. Afterwards, having visualized Yamāntaka—the Lord of the Maṇḍala Circle—arisen from his own seed-syllable within its heart, and having performed the invocation of the Wisdom Circle (*jñānacakra*) preceded by the consecration of the eyes and other limbs, and having performed the worship and other rites, one should visualize the syllable *repha* in its mouth and [recite]:
*oṃ agnaye svāhā*.
Thus, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with clarified butter:
*oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāya sarvapāpāni daha svāhā*. [This is for] sesame seeds.
*oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā*. [This is for] *dūrvā* grass.
Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā | [for] unbroken rice grains. Oṃ sarvasampade svāhā | [for] curd-rice.
Oṃ apratihatavajrāya svāhā | [for] kuśa grass.
Oṃ, svāhā to the Bodhi tree; [this is] for the Aśvattha.
Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrakuvera; [this is] for the Nyagrodha. Oṃ, svāhā to Vajrayajña; [this is] for the Audumbara.

Oṃ sahakārāya svāhā | [This is] for the mango tree. Other substances to be offered should also be prepared in the form of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) according to the instructions, accompanied by the mantra of one’s chosen deity and the words of invocation, and then offered as an oblation (homa). Then, having sprinkled water and offered water for sipping (ācamana) and so forth, having presented fragrant flowers and the like, clothing, and betel leaf, and having made the request for one’s desired aim, one should dismiss [the deity] with the three-syllable mantra ending in *muḥ*. Having offered the remaining substances into the fire, one should dismiss that [fire] as well according to the previous procedure.
Thus ends the fire offering.

The *pātrī* (offering ladle) is one cubit (*hasta*) in length; at its base it is joined with a six-finger-width vajra-gem, and above it is four fingers wide, joined with a vajra set into a two-finger-width cavity, and joined with a vajra in the shape of a four-finger-width lotus petal. It is provided with a channel for the flow of the finest liquid. The *sruva* (dipping-spoon) is two fingers wide, joined with a vajra set into a one-finger-width cavity, and shaped like a lotus petal.
Thus are the *pātrī* and *sruva*.

[7. Pratiṣṭhā] Then, on the ground of consecration—which is enchanting with various parasols, banners, flags, diverse musical instruments, and so forth—the preceptor, adorned with all appropriate ornaments, should place before him the image, the cloth painting, the manuscript, or the reliquary as the case may be. Having presented the sprinkling water, the *argha* offering, and the water for rinsing the mouth, he should take mustard seeds in his left and right fists, whirl them in a clockwise and counter-clockwise motion in front of the image and so forth, and cast them into the fire while reciting: *oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajrāya sarvapāpaṃ daha svāhā*.
With this mantra, one should wave three bowls of *nīrājana* and perform the circumambulation.
Afterwards, taking water in the hollowed palms (*añjali*), one should likewise pour it into the fire.

Then, having worshipped the Tathāgatas abiding in space with the five offerings, and being free from all conceptual constructions, one should take a censer and request those Tathāgatas to remain present.
Having recited three times, "You are the pledge; I am the pledge," [one should think]:
"Just as all the perfectly awakened ones are established in Tuṣita..."
May they remain here in this form, just as they were within the womb of Queen Māyā.
Remaining here constantly as our protectors, please accept these flowers and other offerings for the sake of [the donor named] so-and-so, in order to increase the spirit of enlightenment.
Thereafter,
one should perform the praise with the words beginning, "You are of the nature of Mohavajra," and so forth. Thus concludes the consecration of the deity (devatādhivāsanā).

At dawn, one should bathe the image, which is wrapped in yellow cloth and facing the east. The procedure for this is as follows: having smeared it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated by the seed-syllables *oṃ hūṃ trāṃ hrīḥ aḥ*, one should then [anoint it] with fragrant oil.

With the mantra "Oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyaviśodhana svāhā," one should apply an ointment of *dūrvā* grass and *kuñcikā* seeds. One should remove the oil with the five barks (*pañcavalkala*) placed in a bronze vessel. Immediately thereafter, beginning with the *vijaya* flask, one should bathe [the image] with the water from each of the flasks individually, just as all the Tathāgatas were bathed immediately after their birth.
In that manner, I shall bathe you with pure, divine water.

Immediately thereafter, with the mantra *oṃ sarvatathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūṃ*, one should invoke the assembly of vidyās such as Carcikā situated in space, and visualize her being consecrated by them with jars filled with the water of the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*). Then, having drained the water using a cloth, one should place it before oneself.
One should likewise bathe a cloth painting, a manuscript, or a large stūpa in a mirror according to the previous procedure.
Thus concludes the sequence of the ritual bath.

Then, having visualized the empowerment of the eyes and so forth, as well as the status of the crown of the Lord of the Family (*kulapati*), one should attend to the Tathāgatas situated in the sky in the form of the maṇḍala circle, offer the water for honor (*argha*) and other gifts, cause them to enter the pledge (*samaya*), transform them into the form of syllables within the book, and clothe it with a garment using the mantra:
*oṃ vajravāsase svāhā*. Thereafter, one should present flowers and other offerings.
Oṃ vajrapuṣpe hūṃ! Thus,
this supreme flower of yours, whether born of water or born of land—
This has been given to me with supreme devotion; please accept it as you please.
This supreme fragrance of yours—both innate and produced by combination—is offered by me with the highest devotion; accept it as you please.
This is your supreme incense, both innate and compounded;
offered by me with supreme devotion, accept it as you please.
With a serene mind, I offer this lamp with ghee or oil, possessing divine flames that dispel darkness, for the complete pacification of all ignorance.

I offer this sacrificial food (naivedya), complete with all its components and endowed with various kinds of solid and soft foods, possessed of excellent color, fragrance, and taste; please accept it.
With these mantras, one should offer flowers and other articles. Afterwards, one should open the eyes of the image, taking clarified butter and honey from the Rūpadhātu and using a golden needle:
*oṃ cakṣuś cakṣuḥ samantacakṣurviśodhane svāhā*.
With this mantra, then, brandishing the vajra with the right hand and ringing the bell with the left,
one should perform the praise beginning with "You are the very nature of Mohavajra," and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for consecration.

[9. Preparation of the Disciples] When, being under the sway of compassion, one desires to gather disciples through empowerments and other rites, then, outside the mandala house, one should encourage the qualified disciples—those endowed with noble lineage, physical beauty, youth, faith, learning, renunciation, and so forth—who have performed prostrations before the mandala and hold flowers in their hands; and furthermore, even those who lack such qualities, provided they have gone for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha and abide in the ten paths of virtuous action, by means of a discourse on the Dharma.
The Tathāgatas have correctly taught the ritual for all four assemblies who are engaged in their own training, provided they possess the Mahāyāna mindset.
For some indeed enter the maṇḍala for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi,
while others seek merit and are intent upon the world beyond.
Having cultivated great faith for the sake of the next world, the wise person should enter [the path],
abandoning the fruits of this world and seeking the fruits of the next world.
Since worldly prosperity is abundant, yet that which pertains to the next world is superior to the worldly,
therefore, with steady minds, act for the sake of supreme accomplishment.
Having spoken thus, having caused [the disciple] to enter within himself, and having purified him as the vajra-lotus, he should make this request:
"You are my teacher, the Great Passionate One.
O Great Lord, I desire the firm method of great awakening."
Grant me the commitment; grant me the reality and the thought of awakening.
Grant me the Triple Refuge: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
O Protector, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.

Having recited this three times, and having designated one among the devoted disciples as the principal, he should say: "Come, child! I shall correctly teach you the method of the Mahāyāna, the practice of mantras; for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Way."
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras.
By means of this incomparable application of mantra,
the exceedingly terrible and mighty army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having conformed to worldly custom and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained nirvana;
therefore, my child, apply this mind toward the attainment of omniscience.
Having thus given the threefold instruction, one should generate the unarisen *bodhicitta* and cause those who have already generated it to remember it.

Then, having protected them, one should place the seed-syllables upon them: a *vajra* at their hearts with the syllable *HŪṂ*, a *padma* at their throats with the syllable *ĀḤ*, and a *cakra* on their heads with the syllable *OṂ*. Reciting *HŪṂ ĀḤ OṂ*, one should smear their heart, head, and throat with scented water using the *vajra-muṣṭi* (vajra-fist). Then, one should offer flowers on their heads, incense before them, perfume at their hearts, and a lamp in front of them. All of this is consecrated by reciting the *sārvakarmika-mantra*.

Then, one should offer a tooth-stick made of *aśvattha* or other suitable wood—free from defects such as being split—and with its tip adorned with flowers. Standing facing the east, they chew it and then cast it upon ground smeared with cow-dung to the extent of a *gocarma*. Then, one should announce to them the attainment of pacification (*śānti*) and so forth based on where that [tooth-stick] falls.
Next, having performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), one should give them three mouthfuls of water to drink:
*Oṃ hrīḥ, O pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ.*

With this mantra, one should provide *kuśa* grass for the pillow of the bed. One should protect it with a binding of *dūrvā* grass using a thread three times the length of that [bed], over which the *sarvakarmika-mantra* has been recited. Furthermore:
"When does the appearance of the Omniscient Ones ever occur in the world, or does it not?
It may happen only once in a great while, like the flower of the *udumbara* tree."
Even more difficult to arise than that is the way of mantra practice,
by which those who have entered it are able to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings.
Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons,
all of that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a mandala.
How much more so for one who abides in the system of mantra practice and possesses infinite renown;
for such a person indeed attains the unsurpassed state through the recitation of the mantras of the Protectors.
Cut off for them are the miserable states, the source of all suffering,
for those whose minds are utterly unwavering in this supreme conduct.
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains,
in that you have been gathered here into this teaching by all the Victors together with their sons.
All of you, as soon as you are born, are taken into the care of the Great Beings,
by whom you shall indeed become well-born in the Mahāyāna.
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna; by means of it, you shall go forth and become Tathāgatas.

Having given this instruction, one should have them lie down upon a bed of *kuśa* grass, saying: "Whatever you see in your dreams, you shall tell me at dawn. If they report an inauspicious omen, then one should suppress it with the *sārvakarmika* mantra.
Having protected them once more, one should cause them to take the vows, and having bestowed the irreversible consecration (*avaivartika-satseka*) within the wheel, [one says]: "O Lord, speak to me!"
The reality of the wheel and its deities, and the ritual service for the preceptor.
I shall always be the preceptor for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, [observing] the commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow.

Having had this recited, the preceptor himself subsequently enters the mandala according to the ritual for the entrance of disciples. After performing all the empowerments and obtaining permission, he should take the disciple—who has been given a sacrificial fee outside the curtain and is visualized in the form of Vairocana—and, having had him grasp a flower garland, bind his eyes with a blindfold while reciting the mantra: *ĀḤ KHAṂ VĪRA HŪṂ*.
Having sprinkled [the candidate] with water over which the *sārvakarmika* mantra has been recited, he should ask for the purpose of entering the mandala:
"Who are you, O lover of delight?
He too should reply:
"I am fortunate, O Great Bliss!
Immediately thereafter: "Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga."
Thus one should generate the yoga-mind. Then, one should place the vajra with a flower at the heart with this [mantra]:
*oṃ surate samayas tvaṃ hoḥ siddhya vajra yathāsukham*.
Thus.
Then, having caused [the disciple] to enter behind the curtain with the previously mentioned five-syllable mantra, one should speak as follows:

"Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas; therefore, I shall generate in you the Vajra-wisdom, by means of which wisdom you will attain even the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments. You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala, lest your samaya be violated."
Thus it is said. Then, having placed the vajra upon the head, one should speak as follows:
"This is your samaya-vajra; it shall split your head if you should speak of this to anyone.
Then...
Vajrasattva himself is now established within your heart;
he would depart at that very moment, piercing through it, if you were to speak this method.
Having thus caused him to take an oath, water mixed with sandalwood, saffron, and other substances is consecrated seven times with the mantra *oṃ vajrodaka ṭhaḥ*.
This water of hell shall burn you for transgressing the pledge; through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment. Drink this water of vajra-amrita.
Reciting this, he should make [the disciple] drink it. Then this should be said:

"From this day forward, I am your Vajrapāṇi; whatever I tell you to do, that must be performed by you. You must not disregard me, lest through failing to avoid calamity, you should meet your end and fall into hell.
Thus.

Then, having caused [the disciple] to recite: "May all the Tathāgatas bestow their empowerment; may Vajrasattva enter me," one visualizes upon his head the water-maṇḍala, white and circular, marked with a vase and arisen from the syllable *vaṃ*; therein is *haḥ*. In the heart is the Mahendra-maṇḍala, yellow and square, marked at its corners with three-pronged vajras and arisen from *laṃ*; therein is *hūṃ*. At the navel is the fire-maṇḍala, red with sharp flames, triangular, and arisen from *raṃ*; therein is *āḥ*.

Below the feet, one should meditate upon the wind-mandala, which is blue, moving, shaped like a bow, marked with banners at its corners, and possessing a body of intense, unbearable flames; it is impelled there by the wind until it reaches the other fire-mandala, which in turn, beyond that, ignites the great Indra-mandala with its exceedingly fierce flames.

Then, while the disciple is being satiated by showers of nectar flowing from the Varuṇa-maṇḍala and is being raised up by the wind, [the master], his body intensely agitated by a great display of wrathful pride, brandishing a vajra with his right hand, should cause the descent [of the deity] by offering incense and reciting the descent-mantra (*āveśamantra*). This is the mantra:
Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 āveśaya stobhaya ra ra ra ra cālaya cālaya hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ hūṃ phaṭ.
By this, he enters quickly. Then, having instantly visualized him in the form of Rāgavajrayamāri, and having meditated on a red syllable ĀḤ upon his tongue, one should say to him: "Tarry, O Vajra!"
O Vajradharma, Great Lord Amitābha, Great Bliss!
Speak, O child of great passion; I ask concerning what is auspicious and inauspicious.

With this [mantra], one should question. And when possessed, he speaks of the auspicious and the inauspicious through the paralysis of speech (*vāk-stobha*). Through the paralysis of mind (*citta-stobha*), he knows what has occurred in the three worlds. Through the paralysis of body (*kāya-stobha*), he flies up into the sky. If he flies far, then one should visualize him as having stepped upon the great Maheśvara-maṇḍala above his head, which is marked by a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*); thus he is paralyzed. This is the possession (*āveśa*).
Then, having taken up a flower, he should cast it [into the mandala] with the mantra: *pratīccha vajra hoḥ*.

Whichever deity’s emblem, or its vicinity, or the ground [the flower] falls upon, that family one should designate for him. If it falls in the upper section, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is supreme; if in the middle section, it is middling; if in the lower part, it is inferior. If it falls outside the mandala, there is no accomplishment. If it falls outside the mandala, then he should cast it again. If, after doing so three times, it falls in that very same place, then he should exclude him.
Thus concludes the rite of casting the flower.
Then, having taken that thrown garland, one should bind it upon his head while reciting:
"Accept this, O being of great power!"
Then: "Oṃ!
Today Vajrasattva himself, intent upon opening your eyes, shall open all your eyes with the unsurpassed Vajra-eye."
Reciting thus, he should remove that blindfold.
Then, having first announced the name of each deity, he should show the maṇḍala, beginning with the guardian of the eastern gate and ending with the presiding lord.
Thus concludes the entry into the mandala.
[11. The Five Empowerments] Then,
just as Vajrasattva was empowered by the Buddhas of great wisdom, so too [should he be empowered].
O Lord, sprinkle me as well, or grant me a boon.
One should visualize the disciple who has thus made his request being consecrated by those holding a flask, a vajra, Carcikā, and so forth:
"I bestow the great vajra-consecration, honored by the three realms,
which arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas."

Having recited this, and having taken water from the vessel consecrated for all rites with the vajra-fist while reciting "Oṃ vajrābhiṣiñca," one should consecrate the disciple like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Thus concludes the water consecration.

Immediately thereafter, having placed upon the head a crown fashioned from gold, cloth, and so forth, with the previously mentioned mantra, one should visualize the Tathāgatas situated in the expanse of the sky as being established within the crown in the form of the Family Lords (kuleśa).
This is the crown consecration (mukuṭābhiṣeka).
Thereafter, taking up the vajra:
"Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration.
Take this vajra, which is the state of all the Buddhas, for the sake of perfect accomplishment."
Having recited this and touched the heart and other parts with the vajra, one should place the vajra in the right hand.
This is the vajra-consecration.
Then, having placed a bell in the left hand and having caused the disciple to perform the gesture of embracing with both hands joined by a vajra and a vajra-bell, one should recite:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Lord of Vajras; abide, O Vajra, you are the Samaya," and having spoken thus, one should bestow [the bell].
This bell-consecration itself is the consecration of lordship.
Thus concludes the bell consecration.
Then, one should place the vajra and bell upon the head [of the disciple].
Reciting "Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you with the vajra-name-consecration;
O Śrī-[Name]vajra," and so forth, one should bestow a name according to the appropriate family (kula).
By these consecrations, one becomes authorized for the exposition of the mantra-tantras and for the practice of mantra-sādhana.
The fivefold consecration alone is the "crown consecration" (mauliseka), because in all cases, such as those of Carcikā and the others, it functions in the form of the crown consecration.
[12. The Master Initiation] Then, having received the initiation of the crown and having received the vows of the master, one says:
"O treasury of compassion, grant me the initiation of the Vajrācārya."
May I be capable of accomplishing the welfare of both myself and others through your grace.

Having thus been requested, one should seat the petitioner upon a pedestal atop an eight-petaled lotus made with white powder within the vicinity of the maṇḍala; having consecrated him with Vajracarcikā and the others, one should cause him to take the three samayas.
In this regard, the three samayas are as follows:
having meditated on the vajra with the syllable *hūṃ*.
Take up this great sword of the three realms, honored by all the Buddhas,
like another Dharma-sword for conquering the Māras.
Thus, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp the vajra according to its true nature.
This is the Vajra-samaya.
Afterwards, for the sake of accomplishment, take up the bell born from the syllable ĀḤ, which is the very nature of wisdom and means, as well as the vajra-bell;
O child, you are the Vajra— perform the gathering of disciples!
With this [verse], one should place [the object] into his hand:
"Existence is indeed pure by nature, yet it is made to appear as non-existent by [impure] natures;
through beings who are truly pure by nature, the supreme existence is brought about."
With this [mantra], he too should cause [the bell] to sound.
Thus is the commitment of the bell (ghaṇṭāsamaya).
Immediately thereafter,
the mudrā is indeed declared to be the commitment (samaya), because it provides firmness to the mental form;
since it makes every form firm, it is therefore celebrated as "mudrā" (the seal).
By this, one should consecrate the Mahāmudrā as being of the nature of one's own chosen deity.
Thus is the commitment of the mudrā.
Then one should reveal the reality of the mandala, the reality of the deity, the preparation of the preceptor, the accomplishment of the mandala, and the ritual of the preceptor’s entrance.
In that regard, because there is no difference between the awakened and the unawakened in terms of reality, it is square.
The eastern gate is the purification of that faith which consists in the equality of reflections through the inseparability of the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena as being both one and many.

The southern gate is through the purification of the fourfold vigor (*vīrya*), which consists of the exertion, preparation, observation, and internalization for the abandonment of unwholesome states that have arisen and the non-arising of those not yet arisen, as well as for the maintenance and further production of wholesome states that have arisen.
The western gate is through the purification of the mindfulness that pertains to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)—namely, desire, vigor, mind, and investigation.
The northern gate is through the purification of the concentration that pertains to the five faculties (*indriya*)—namely, faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

The first dhyāna has five factors: applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). The second dhyāna is devoid of applied and sustained thought. The third dhyāna is devoid of joy and is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*). The fourth dhyāna is the complete purity of equanimity and mindfulness, as well as the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant; through this purity, it has four archways. Through the purity of the four samādhis—the Śūraṅgama, Gaganagañja, Vimala, and Siṃhavikrīḍita—it has four porticos.

Through the purity of the fourfold dhāraṇīs— of the text, the meaning, the etymology, and eloquence— the host of deities stationed upon the altar is present for the fulfillment of all aspirations, adorned with every variety of ornament. Furthermore, through the purity of the ninefold teaching consisting of the Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Jātaka, Vaipulya, and Adbhutadharma, it takes the form of instruction for those to be trained, appearing like a banner with the sound of tinkling bells stirred by the wind.

Through the purification of the seven factors of enlightenment—namely mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity—he is radiant with necklaces, half-necklaces, mirrors, flower garlands, strings of flowers, and yak-tail whisks.

The first liberation is when one perceives internal forms by way of the signless and wishless aspects regarding external forms. The second is when one perceives internal forms in that same manner while having the perception of external forms. The third is when, having directly realized and attained the perception of both internal and external forms, one dwells therein. The fourth is the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite space. The fifth is the meditative attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

The attainment of the sphere of nothingness is the sixth; the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the seventh; the attainment of cessation is the eighth. Thus, through the purification of the eight liberations, there is the hub of the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*).
Because of the turning of the wheel of Dharma according to the Vajra Way, it is joined with vajra-lines attached to the upper surface of the hub of the universal vajra.
By way of the differentiation of the results, the twenty-spoked universal vajra pierces the twenty peaks of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Due to the distinction between the support and the supported, the wall-panel of the ground is five-colored.
Its nature is non-adhesive, and by virtue of manifesting as both one and many, it appropriately serves as the seat of a thousand-petaled lotus in the locations of the deities.
Because it ripens the *bodhicitta*, it is endowed with a solar seat.
By way of nourishing the sprout of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), it is endowed with a moon seat;
it is a lamp of the Dharma-torch, filled with the nectar of compassion in eight vases;
its fragrance is fame.
The food offering consists of the *dharmāhāra*.
Thus ends the definition of the reality of the mandala.
Now, the definition of the reality of the deity is also being stated.
In that regard, the Blessed One is the purity of the consciousness-element, which is the perfectly pure dharmadhātu-consciousness within the great hatred of the aggregate of consciousness.
Because he gathers together all the stains of affliction in the world and brings about the end of Yama,
he is Yamāri.
Because gentleness is not effective toward those who are extremely wicked and fierce, he possesses great wrath (*mahākrodha*).
Through the purity of the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*), he has three faces (*trimukha*).
He has six arms because his nature is the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
His hands hold a vajra and other implements because he destroys the various faults such as stinginess (*mātsarya*).
He wears ornaments of serpents because [the serpents] represent the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are a portion of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Because he has fulfilled the two accumulations, he is embraced by his own consort, Prajñā.

Due to his constant intention to act for the benefit of sentient beings, even while possessing the Dharmakāya in the form of unsurpassed innate bliss, he manifests in the non-dual forms of the Sambhogakāya and Nirmāṇakāya.
The Blessed One Mohayamāri is the purification of the aggregate of form, great delusion, and the mirror-like wisdom.
Furthermore, as before, he is adorned with the secondary afflictions that are portions of delusion;
the Blessed One Piśunavajrayamāri is purified by the knowledge of equanimity, which is the great slanderer of the aggregate of feeling.
The remainder is as before, adorned with the secondary afflictions that are portions of pride.
The Yamāri of Passion is purified by the wisdom of discerning the great passion of the aggregate of perception;
he is adorned with the secondary afflictions that are portions of passion.
The Blessed One, the Yamāri of Envy, is purified by the performance of activities through the great envy of the aggregate of mental formations.
Adorned with the secondary affliction that is a portion of envy;
the adversary of the Māra of the aggregates, which is the obscuration of the knowable consisting of the view of a self-identity;
the Blessed One, purified by the power of faith, is Mudgarayamāri.
He is adorned with secondary afflictions that are favorable to the discordant factors;
he is the adversary of the Māra of the afflictions, which are the obscuration of the affliction of the view of extremes;
the Blessed One is purified by the power of vigor and is the slayer of the staff-bearing Māra.

The Blessed One Padmayamāri is adorned with secondary afflictions that are favorable to his adversaries; he is the adversary of wrong views, karmic obscurations, death, and Māra, and is purified through the power of mindfulness.
He is adorned with secondary afflictions that conform to the discordant factors;
he is the adversary of the Māra of the Son of Heaven, who causes the obstruction and distraction born from the adherence to views.
The Blessed One Khaḍgayamāri is purified by the power of meditative concentration.

Vajracarcikā has as her nature the great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), the perfection of skillful means (*upāyapāramitā*), and the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*), adorned with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) pertaining to her own objective sphere.
Vajravārāhī has as her nature the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*), and the water element (*apdhātu*).

Vajrasarasvatī has the nature of the perfection of great joy (*mahāmuditā*), which is the vow-perfection (*praṇidhānapāramitā*) of the fire element. Vajragaurī has the nature of the perfection of equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), which is the gnosis-perfection (*jñānapāramitā*) of the wind element.
The four skulls [on her head] represent the external purity of form and the other sense objects.
Because odor is included within form,
and because the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is omnipresent,
the ten stages (daśabhūmi) should be understood as corresponding respectively to the purification of the ten perfections (daśapāramitā).

The qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) arise precisely here through the destruction of their respective opposites; however, they are not written out here for fear of excessive length.
Thus ends the definition of the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*).

Thus, the purification of the preceptor (*ācārya-parikarma*), the observance of the rules regarding what is to be protected, and the observance of the rules regarding what is to be consumed must be understood according to the Tantra. Furthermore, the protection, the *praty-aṅgiras*, the accomplishment of the mandala, and the characteristics of the preceptor’s entrance have been explained.

In that regard, the preceptor, joined with the fourfold yoga, should place before him a great sound of music and a bali-offering consisting of various kinds of foods—solid, soft, chewable, drinkable, and lickable—as well as perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, bells, and flags, all contained within carts, loads, and baskets.

Or even if it is only three handfuls of water accompanied by a mere morsel of food; then, having emanated the divine wrathful deities holding nooses and goads in their hands, one should visualize them piercing the heart with the goad and binding [the victim] by the throat with the noose as they are being brought forth. Therein, with the mantra:

*Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 duṣṭendraṃ saparivāram ākarṣaya jaḥ*, one should thus summon Indra—the thousand-eyed, fair and white-complexioned one, seated upon an elephant, with a vajra and a threatening gesture in his right and left hands.

Having first established [the deities], one should establish Upendra with that same mantra to his immediate left: black in color, mounted upon Garuḍa, wearing a jeweled crown, holding a mace and a discus in his right hands, and holding a conch and the Kaustubha gem in his left. Then, not too far to his left, one should establish Yama: blue in color, seated upon a buffalo, with tawny hair blazing upward, holding a staff and making the *tarjanī* gesture with his hands, positioned in the southern direction.

Again, with that same [mantra], one should establish Varuṇa in the west—white, mounted on a serpent, and holding a snake-noose in his hand. Again, with that same [mantra], one should establish Kuvera in the north—yellow, standing upon a treasure, corpulent, and holding a citron and a mongoose in his hands. Right there, with that same mantra, one should establish Sauṇḍa in the south—white, mounted on a mouse, holding a rosary and a battle-axe in his right hands, and a root and a water-pot in his left hands.

Again, with that same [mantra], having established Īśāna in the northeast—white, mounted on a bull, wearing matted hair, three-eyed, holding a trident, and with two hands embracing Gaurī who holds a skull-cup; again, with that same [mantra], having established Agni in the southeast—red, seated upon a goat, with a rosary and a water-pot in his hands;
and again, with that same [mantra], having established Rākṣasa in the southwest—blue, mounted on a corpse, holding a knife and a skull-cup in his hands, fierce and wrathful.

Again, with that same [mantra], he establishes in the northwest direction Vāyu, smoke-colored and stout, mounted on a deer, wearing a wind-cloth; again, with that same [mantra], he establishes above Candra, white, seated upon a chariot of night-lotuses, holding night-lotuses;
again, with that same mantra, he establishes above that Bhānu, red, holding two lotuses with his two hands, seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses.

Again, with that same [mantra], one should establish above him the god Brahmā—fair-complexioned, four-faced, holding a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*), the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and a staff, adorned with matted locks, and seated upon a swan.

Again, with that same [mantra], one should establish below him the goddess Earth—yellow, seated upon a lotus, holding a jar in her left hand and making the gesture of assent (*pratijñābhyupagama*) with her right hand.

Again, with that same [mantra], one should establish right there Vemacitrin—blue, seated upon a chariot, with his sword and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) in his left and right hands respectively.

Then again, having projected from one’s own heart wrathful deities in the form of Yamāntaka, holding stakes and possessing wrathful necks, one should nail them to the heart, throat, head, and the base of the feet with this very mantra:
*oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 sarvaduṣṭendrādīn saparivārān kīlaya hūṃ phaṭ*.
Immediately after the nailing, they all become like Yamāntaka in appearance, or take the form of the fluid of bodhicitta, as if by contact with an alchemical elixir.

In that regard, if they are of liquid form, they are produced according to the sequence of seed-syllables and signs. Therein, Indra is produced from the syllable *hrīḥ* and the vajra; he is fair-complexioned, with a blue face on the right and a white one on the left, wears a jewel crown, holds a skull-cup with his two principal arms, and holds a vajra, sword, lotus, and wheel with his remaining four arms; he stands upon a moon. Yama is produced from the staff [and] the syllable *ṣṭrīḥ*; he is blue, with a white face on the right and a red one on the left; he holds a hand-axe, a staff, and a sword in his right hands, and a skull-cup, a lotus, and a wheel in his left hands; his hair is tawny and blazing upward, he has the sun as his seat, and possesses the form of a great wrathful deity.

Varuṇa is produced from the seed-syllable *vi* and the *nāga*-noose; he is white in color, with faces that are blue on the right and red on the left. His right hands hold a sword, a *kartri*, and a *nāga*-noose, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a lotus, and a wheel. He wears a jewel crown, stands upon the moon, and is seated upon a tortoise. Kuvera is produced from the seed-syllable *kṛ*; he is yellow in color, with faces that are blue on the right and white on the left. His right hands hold a sword, a *bījapūraka* fruit, and a *kartri*, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a wheel, and a lotus. He is corpulent, wears a jewel crown, and stands upon the moon.

Īśāna is produced from the syllable *takāra* and a trident; he is white in color, with faces that are blue on the right and red on the left. His right hands hold a flaying knife, a trident, and a sword, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a jewel, and a wheel. He embraces his own consort Gaurī and stands upon the moon. Agni is produced from the syllable *ākāra* and a water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*); he has faces that are red on the right and white on the left. His right hands hold a flaying knife, a water-pot, and a sword, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a lotus, and a jewel. He stands upon the sun as his seat.

Nairṛti, produced from the syllable *Na*, is blue in color and wrathful in form; he has white and red faces on the right and left, respectively, and holds a *kartṛ* (cleaver), a vajra, and a sword in his right hands, while holding a skull-cup, a lotus, and a wheel in his left; he stands upon a solar seat. Vāyu, born from the garment of the syllable *Na*, is smoke-colored; he has blue and white faces on the right and left, respectively, and holds a *kartṛ*, a wind-banner, and a sword in his right hands, while holding a skull-cup, a jewel, and a lotus in his left; he stands upon the moon. Candra, produced from the *kumuda* (water-lily) of the syllable *Hūṃ*, is white in color; he has blue and red faces on the right and left, respectively, and holds a *kartṛ* and a *kumuda* in his right hands, and a skull-cup, a jewel, and a wheel in his left hands.

From the syllable *HŪṂ* arises the Sun, red in color, with faces that are blue on the right and white on the left; his right hands hold a flaying knife, a lotus, and a sword, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a jewel, and a wheel; he stands upon the moon. From the syllable *PHAṬ* arises Brahmā, yellow in color, with faces that are blue on the right and white on the left; his right hands hold a flaying knife, a rosary, and a sword, while his left hands hold a skull-cup, a jewel, and a lotus; he stands upon the moon.

From the syllable *PHAṬ* arises the Earth Goddess, yellow in color, with faces that are blue on the right and white on the left; her right hands hold a flaying knife, a vase, and a sword, while her left hands hold a skull-cup, a jewel, and a lotus; she stands upon the moon.

Vemacitrī, produced from the syllable *Svā*, is blue in color; he has faces that are white and red on the right and left respectively, holds a curved knife (*kartṛ*), a sword, and a scimitar in his right hands, and a skull-cup, a wheel, and a lotus in his left hands; he stands upon the sun. From the syllable *Hā* arise Viṣṇu and Sauṇḍa. Therein, Viṣṇu, born from the mace (*gadā*), is blue, white, and red on his right and left faces respectively; he holds a curved knife, a mace, and a sword in his right hands, and carries a skull-cup, a wheel, and a lotus in his left hands; he stands upon the moon. Sauṇḍa, born from the battle-axe (*paraśu*), is white; he has faces that are white and red on the right and left respectively, holds a curved knife, a battle-axe, and a sword in his right hands, and carries a skull-cup, a wheel, and a lotus in his left hands; he stands upon the moon.

Thus, having contemplated that all [the deities] have bodies in which their own wisdom has become non-dual, and that with their two principal arms—equipped with a curved knife (*kartṛ*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*)—they intend to embrace [the consort], standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and that all are those who accomplish the desires of the practitioner; |||

Having generated within their eyes and other sense organs the vajra-eyes and so forth as previously described, and having likewise generated the body-vajras and so forth within their bodies, one should contemplate their state of being crowned by Yamāntaka through the aforementioned consecrations. Then, having offered the water for welcoming (*argha*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), and subsequently having prepared the entire offering of oblations (*balis*) according to the sequence of the *Amṛtasādhana*, one should consecrate it with the three principles (*tritattva*). Furthermore, having visualized the application of the tongue-vajra for them, one should then present that nectar with this mantra.

Oṃ, to Indra, Hrīḥ! To Yama, Ṣṭrīḥ! To Varuṇa, Vi! To Kubera, Kṛ! To Īśāna, Ta! To Agni, Ā! To Nairṛti, Na! To Vāyu, Na! To Candra, Hūṃ! To Arka, Hūṃ! To Brahmā, Phaṭ! To Vasundharā, Phaṭ! To Vemacitrin, Svā! To all beings, Hā! Hā hṇī 2 hūṃ 2 pheṃ 2 svāhā!

Afterwards, one should offer flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings, and so forth. Those [deities], being well-pleased with the practitioner, partake of all the enjoyments, such as tasting and the like.
Then, brandishing the vajra and gracefully sounding the vajra-bell, one should praise them:
"You are the very nature of Mohavajra."
With these and other [verses], one should subsequently inform them of one's intention and dismiss them with: Oṃ āḥ hūṃ muḥ.
By this [means], they too, having accomplished everything according to the practitioner's desire preceded by the utterance of *jyotir-jyot*, depart to perform the welfare of the world.
Thus ends the section on the bali offering.
Thereafter, having taken hold of this disciple in the form of Yamamathana, one should grant him the authorization:
"For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, throughout all worlds and in every way,
turn the wheel of Dharma for the universe according to their discipline."
Having inserted the words "Vajra, Ratna, Padma, Karma" in place of "Dharma," [the names are formed] sequentially with five verses.
Thus ends the granting of permission.
This is that state of all buddhahood, which resides in the hand of Vajrasattva;
you too must always uphold it, O Vajrapāṇi of firm vows.

Thus, while bestowing the vajra, [the master] should cause the disciple to undertake the vajra-vow as he recites: "Oṃ, O Vajrasattva, abide in the samaya of the vajra of the siddhi of all Tathāgatas; I uphold you! Hī hī hī hī hūṃ!"
Thus concludes the bestowal of the vajra vow.

Then, having meditated on oneself as the form of the Buddha, with the left fist at the heart in the gesture of grasping the tip of the corner of the robe, and with the right hand in the boon-granting (*varada*) mudrā,
[one says]: *Oṃ, here I prophesy you, O Vajrasattva.*
[13. Secret Initiation] O Khavajra and the others, grant it to me!

Or one may request [the empowerment] with one of these verses. Then the Guru, manifesting the fourfold union (*caturyoga*), extracts from the disciple’s mouth the [wisdom] established in self-awareness—which was produced within the vajra that has moved into the interior of the lotus of *dharmatā*—and, having pressed it together by means of the Nameless and the Eldest [fingers], places it in the disciple’s mouth:
“This jewel of drink is indeed the accomplisher of the body-vajra;
let it be drunk! O child, you are always Wisdom itself; [drink] the water of the mind.”
With this [verse], he should place Makaranda;
he too, saying "Oh, what bliss!", should draw him in and place him within the waves of his own enjoyment. She too, having risen, should place there that which remains of her own lotus.
Thus concludes the secret initiation.
[14. The Empowerment of Wisdom-Knowledge (Prajñājñānābhiṣeka):

Immediately thereafter, for the disciple who has requested [the empowerment] with the previously mentioned verse in order to directly realize the knowledge of mere self-awareness—either with that same [consort] or another—the [master], placing her hand in his hand, says:
"This delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated; it was devised by the Buddhas."
Through the yoga of passion for the wheel, experience the true bliss.
Buddhahood is not attained by any other means, and these three worlds are pure;
therefore, never bring about separation from this within saṃsāra.
This is that unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
for the fool who transgresses it, there shall be no supreme accomplishment.
Having said this, she should give [the lotus].

She, too, displaying a blooming, naked lotus that is smeared with sandalwood, saffron, and the like, adorned above with a garland of exceedingly fragrant flowers, and very clearly manifest, should say this to the disciple:
"My child, are you able to consume feces, urine, and so forth?"
Tell me, my child, as you please: [the nature of] blood, semen, and likewise flesh; the devotion of women, and furthermore, the kissing of the lotus of the womb.
Thus he said:
"O Queen, why should I not venture to consume excrement, urine, and the like?
One must always show devotion to women, as well as kissing and [the enjoyment of] their vulvas."
Thus she should say:
"O, for him who serves my lotus— which is endowed with all happiness—
according to the prescribed rite, I stand before him."
O Padmā, perform whatever task is required, such as the propitiation of the Perfectly Awakened One;
for the King of Great Bliss himself is always present right here.
"Devote yourself to liberation! Hoḥ!
Having thus obtained Vajradhātvīśvarī through the guru’s instruction, the yogi performs specific ritual actions;
as long as he does not release the *bodhicitta*, [the practice continues].
In that state, one attains an uninterrupted, indescribable bliss born of joy.
But when the thought of awakening— the treasury of all accomplishments— has fallen,
and when the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, how can there be irreproachable accomplishment?
From the union of the vajra and the element of space, and from their contact, a most wonderful bliss arises; that which produces supreme bliss.

Between the two joys of cessation (*viramānanda*), observe the target and make it firm at the point of pressure between the lotus and the excellent jewel-vajra. Gazing at the mind as it has entered within the jewel from the vajra-posture (*vajraparyaṅka*).
That cognition which arises is of the nature of that [object]; enough of this.
Neither passion nor dispassion, nor even the middle way, is perceived;
when the yogi’s vision is thus through knowledge, he abides in bliss and does not leak away.
Through the application of knowledge, one may remain for a watch, or a single day, a fortnight, a month, a year, a kalpa, or even a thousand kalpas.

Having reflected thus and maintained [the practice] according to one's ability, one should release [the seed-syllable], extract it from the lotus with the tongue alone, and grasp the bodhicitta in the form of the samaya by means of the vision of reality.
Thus concludes the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).
Now, how is it that the five empowerments and the empowerment of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) are not indeed revealed here?
First, by means of the crown empowerment (*mauliseka*), one should take up the sword as the second.
The third is the vajra-bell, and the fourth is the consumption of the moon;
these four great consecrations emerged from the mouth of Kṛṣṇa.
Because of this statement in the *Tantra*:

"This is true. The five initiations alone constitute the crown initiation (*mauliseka*), because in all cases [the deities] such as Vajracarcikā and others function by way of being sprinkled upon the crown. Furthermore, it is so because of its primacy in conferring authority over all rites.
The bestowal of the Vajra-samaya is the sword initiation (*khaḍgābhiṣeka*), because it cuts through all opposing factors.

In the *Avaivartyābhiṣekaprakāśita* itself, having added the empowerment of the body (*mūrtyadhiṣṭhāna*) within the commitment (*samaya*) of the vajra and bell, as well as the vows, prophecies, and assurances taught in the general tantras,
there is also the empowerment of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*).
Having assumed the form of Vārāhī, all women are desired.
Then, having seen the banner and the path, one should prepare milk there.
With a mind focused solely on the practice of milk, one should accomplish the Mahāmudrā.
Thus it has indeed been established.

That very [reality], being free from the stain of conceptualization regarding the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire unsurpassed world, shines forth as inseparable from one's own self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) whose nature is a circle of rays emanating from a jewel, one should give it to the disciple through speech in its designated form; this is the "giving again.
Thereafter, one should encourage the disciples with praise and inspire them.
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today completely liberated from all sins and well-established.
There is no further death for you from this Great Bliss Vehicle;
invincible and unbound, rejoice, free from fear from any quarter.
The suffering of existence has ceased for you, for the sake of ultimate purification from existence;
you have become the foremost of teachers for the sake of the ultimate accomplishment of liberation from existence.
This perfected commitment and vow must be constantly guarded by you;
it is the supreme, eternal command proclaimed by all the Buddhas together.
The teachers are not to be despised, and one must not transgress the command of the Sugata.
Likewise, out of anger toward one's brothers, one should not proclaim their faults.
One must never abandon a mind of loving-kindness toward sentient beings;
one should not forsake the thought of awakening, nor should one disparage the Dharma of oneself or others.
One should never reveal the secret to beings who have not been ripened;
one should certainly not disparage one's own aggregates, nor should one find fault with the dharmas of existence.
One should always abandon corrupt friendship and must never disregard the teachings of the Dharma;
one should certainly not deceive a faithful being and should always observe the commitments.
Because of the fault inherent in defiling women, whose very nature is wisdom,
the yogi should neither wander for alms nor abandon his yoga.
One should always and constantly recite the mantra, and one should always observe the pledges and other commitments.
If, through negligence, one should commit an offense against the guru or violate the samaya,
then, having indeed drawn the mandala, one should confess the misdeed before the Sugatas.
Today your birth has become fruitful, since you are well-established in this;
you shall become equal to the gods of the [four] ages, of this—there is no doubt.
Today you have been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders;
may you remain steadfast as sovereign lords over the great kingdom of the three realms.
Having conquered the Māras today, you have entered the supreme city;
Buddhahood has been attained by you this very day—of this there is no doubt.
Thus, fashion the diamond of a serene mind; practice your own commitment which bestows inexhaustible bliss.
Today, in this world of fleeting pleasures, [rely upon] Vajrasattva—
You have attained the state of peerless permanence.
Having prostrated at the feet of the guru, the disciples, who are devoted and affectionate toward the virtuous, should say: "O Lord, we shall do exactly as you command."

If it is possible, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) by means of fire-oblation (*homa*), having grasped the right thumb of those [initiates] with the left hand. Having offered one, three, or seven *pūrṇāhuti* oblations, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be requested. They too, with joyful minds, bestow according to their means land, elephants, horses, gold, ornaments, sons, wives, and so forth; or they grant assistance for one's own success, or the acquisition of qualities such as learning and the rest.

Then, having satisfied the disciples and received their respective fees, one should worship the *cakra* with all kinds of food and drink, both one's own and those of others. Having taken worthy disciples and gratified them with various supreme offerings, one should conclude the rite.
Then, having performed the worship, praise, and tasting of the nectar (*amṛta*), and having made the formal request, one should maintain a firm sense of identity with the deity.
Reciting, "All phenomena are unarisen; all phenomena are non-existent," one should cast the wheel with vajra-tips.
Then, having given a small amount of dust to those who request it, one should cast the remainder into great water.
"Whatever wealth is [obtained] during the filling of the pit, the consecration, the fire offering, and the wheel—all that belongs to the preceptor alone; so said the Holder of the Excellent Vajra."
In the social ritual, [the procedure] was clearly established by Bhadrapāda and others;
however, because the method for constructing the wheel (*cakravidhāna*) here is far more obscure, it requires great effort.
In this regard, the wise should exercise forbearance toward omissions or redundancies,
since such a work as this has been obtained with great difficulty and recorded from my own memory.
Having performed the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala of Śrī Yamamāri, which accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings,
which is the domain of the wise, wherein the mass of activities is inseparable from one’s own gnosis,
which dispels the darkness of all ignorance, and bestows the awakening to the non-duality of existence and peace—
May the world, by means of that store of merit which I have attained, become possessed of the wealth of wisdom.
This *Upāyikā* [commentary] on the mandala of the glorious *Yamāri-tantra* is completed.
This is the work of the teacher Śrīdhara.
In the year ... , on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, this was written during the victorious reign of the illustrious Indradeva. [Scribbles]
